stops.name: Cloud Gate
stops.description: Anish Kapoor's 110-ton mirrored bean, welded from 168 stainless steel plates, throws the whole Michigan Avenue skyline back at whoever is standing under it.

stops.name: Crown Fountain
stops.description: Two glass block towers at the Michigan and Monroe corner of Millennium Park play video portraits of a thousand ordinary Chicagoans, who spit water at the crowd all summer.

stops.name: Jay Pritzker Pavilion
stops.description: Frank Gehry's brushed steel ribbons peel back over the Millennium Park lawn, where a trellis of speakers puts every picnic blanket inside the concert hall.

stops.name: Chicago Cultural Center
stops.description: Chicago's first public library, free to walk into, crowned by a 38-foot Tiffany dome of more than 60,000 pieces of glass.

stops.name: Chicago Theatre
stops.description: The six-story vertical CHICAGO sign over State Street has stood in for the whole city since 1921, and the original marquee below it now belongs to the Smithsonian.

stops.name: Marshall Field and Company Building
stops.description: Generations met under the seven-ton Great Clock at State and Washington; inside, a Tiffany mosaic ceiling of 1.6 million glass pieces caps the southwest atrium.

stops.name: Reliance Building
stops.description: This 1895 tower was the first skyscraper clad mostly in plate glass, making nearly every glass-and-steel building since a descendant of it; it runs as a hotel today.

stops.name: Sullivan Center
stops.description: Louis Sullivan wrapped the rounded corner entrance at State and Madison in cast-iron ornament so dense the building looks like it is floating above the sidewalk.

stops.name: Chicago Picasso
stops.description: The city mocked this 50-foot Cor-Ten figure when it went up in 1967 and now lets children slide down it; Picasso said it was his Afghan hound.

stops.name: Marquette Building
stops.description: Push through the doors for a free lobby of Tiffany glass mosaics and bronze reliefs retelling Father Marquette's 1674 winter on the Chicago River.

stops.name: Flamingo
stops.description: Alexander Calder's 53-foot vermilion arch was set in Federal Plaza specifically to fight the black Miesian boxes around it, and you can walk right underneath it.

stops.name: The Berghoff
stops.description: Open since 1898 and still family run, the Berghoff was handed Chicago liquor license No. 1 the year Prohibition ended and has been renewed on it every year since.

stops.name: Rookery Building
stops.description: Burnham and Root's 1888 block hides a skylit light court that Frank Lloyd Wright remade in white marble, his only work on any building in the Loop.

stops.name: Chicago Board of Trade Building
stops.description: Look straight up LaSalle Street at the faceless 31-foot aluminum Ceres, goddess of grain, holding wheat and corn above the old trading floor.

stops.name: Art Institute of Chicago Building
stops.description: Edward Kemeys' two bronze lions have guarded these Michigan Avenue stairs since 1893, and the city dresses them in team gear whenever Chicago reaches a playoff.

note: Chicago's first run. Every stop sits inside the Loop between Randolph and Jackson, State and LaSalle, so the batch walks as roughly a 1-mile loop starting at Millennium Park. All 15 have a verified street address and a looked-up ZIP. Three stops share the Millennium Park address 201 E Randolph St, ZIP 60601 per the City of Chicago listing rather than the 60602 several directories give, because the park is one postal address while Cloud Gate, Crown Fountain and the Pritzker Pavilion are three separate places inside it. Flamingo is filed at 230 S Dearborn St, the Kluczynski Federal Building it stands in front of, since Federal Plaza has no address of its own and one directory gives it an obviously wrong 60610. Dropped Buckingham Fountain: it is about 0.6 mi south of the cluster and sources split between 60601 and 60605 for 301 S Columbus Dr, so the ZIP could not be settled. Also passed over the demolished landmarks GeoSearch still returns (Masonic Temple, Chicago Federal Building, Garrick Theater, McVicker's Theater, Crosby's Opera House) and the 'L' stations, which are transit rather than places to stand in front of.
